description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of selected Qur'anic suras from the earliest Hijazi-script manuscripts. Contains composition-specific entries (early-manuscript paleography, rasm-vs-Hafs variant conventions, sura-specific lexical items, the Raëlian-canon-citation acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework for Suras 21:1-5, 54:1, 56:15-24) that are not (yet) appropriate for promotion to the central production glossary. Entries here may be promoted to central via the standard overlay→central promotion pattern when they appear in subsequent Islamic-tradition compositions and acquire cross-corpus reach.

entries.lemma: the project-specific rasm-paleographic-convention for the WoH-Translation of the Qur'an from the earliest Hijazi-script manuscripts: (1) the rasm is the bare consonantal skeleton — no iʿjām dots, no tashkīl vowel-marks, no hamza-glyph; (2) hamza-collapse: word-internal hamza glyphs are removed in the rasm rendering (e.g., Hafs السماء becomes rasm السما; Hafs بأكواب becomes rasm باكواب); (3) tāʾ-marbūṭa-as-hāʾ: the tāʾ-marbūṭa (ة) in the modern script appears in the early Hijazi manuscripts as plain hāʾ (ه); (4) defective scripting of long ā in many words (e.g., Hafs ولدان becomes rasm ولدن; Hafs فاكهة becomes rasm فكهه); (5) defective scripting of the hamza-on-alif and hamza-on-wāw and hamza-on-yāʾ throughout
entries.standardEnglish: the rasm-paleographic-convention as the convention for the rasm-field in the source-ar-N.json and chapter-N.json source layers
entries.wohChoice: preserved as a project-internal paleographic-convention; the rasm field reflects the early Hijazi-script orthography; the ar field reflects the modern Cairo Hafs vocalized orthography; both layers are preserved per ayah
entries.rationale:
**The WoH-Translation of the Qur'an preserves three layers per ayah** in the source-ar-N.json and chapter-N.json files: (1) the *rasm* — the bare consonantal skeleton from the earliest-attested Hijazi-script manuscript witnesses (Tübingen Ma VI 165 for Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ; Codex Parisino-petropolitanus for Sūrat al-Qamar and Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah; both radiocarbon-dated 649-675 CE / late 7th c. CE); (2) the modern vocalized Arabic — the Hafs ʿan ʿĀṣim reading-tradition, Cairo recension (1924 King Fuad edition), supplied as the reference vocalization; (3) the scientific transliteration in DMG / ALA-LC convention.

**The rasm-paleographic-convention** preserves the actual scribal content of the early Hijazi manuscripts: (a) no *iʿjām* dots (the dots distinguishing letters of similar consonantal shape — bāʾ / tāʾ / thāʾ / nūn / yāʾ; jīm / ḥāʾ / khāʾ; dāl / ḏāl; rāʾ / zāy; sīn / shīn; ṣād / ḍād; ṭāʾ / ẓāʾ; ʿayn / ghayn; fāʾ / qāf — were added across the 8th-10th centuries CE; the underlying rasm in the earliest manuscripts is substantially what was copied in the 7th century); (b) no *tashkīl* vowel-marks (added in the same period); (c) no *hamza* glyph (added later); (d) the *tāʾ-marbūṭa* (ة) appears as plain *hāʾ* (ه); (e) defective scripting of long ā in many words.

**The convention applies across the three WoH-translated suras** and structures the source-ar-N.json and chapter-N.json file layers. The English translation (i18n.en) reflects the rasm-and-Hafs lexical-semantic content (which is consonant across the early Hijazi witnesses and the Cairo Hafs for the target ayahs; the paleographic differences are scribal-development questions not affecting the English).

Named scholarship: **B. Sadeghi and U. Bergmann**, 'The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet', *Arabica* 57 (2010), 343-436 — the foundational radiocarbon and codicological study of the Sanʿāʾ 1 palimpsest; **B. Sadeghi and M. Goudarzi**, 'Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān', *Der Islam* 87 (2010), 1-129 — the transcription of the Sanʿāʾ 1 lower text; **A. Hilali**, *The Sanaa Palimpsest: The Transmission of the Qur'an in the First Centuries AH* (Oxford 2017); **F. Déroche**, *Qur'ans of the Umayyads* (Brill 2014); *La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus* (Brill 2009); **A. Neuwirth**, *Scripture, Poetry, and the Making of a Community* (Oxford 2014); **G. S. Reynolds** (ed.), *The Qurʾān in Its Historical Context* (Routledge 2008/2011); **Corpus Coranicum** project (Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities) for the digital comparative apparatus.

**Promotion candidate:** if subsequent WoH-Translation Islamic-tradition compositions adopt the same rasm-paleographic-convention, this overlay entry should be promoted to the central glossary as a project-wide convention.

entries.lemma: the project-specific scientific-transliteration convention for Arabic source-text rendering: DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) with ALA-LC (American Library Association / Library of Congress) compatibility; standard underdot for emphatic consonants (ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ ḥ); ḫ for hāʾ-with-dot (kh sound); ġ for ʿayn-with-dot (gh sound); š for shīn; ḏ for ḏāl; ṯ for thāʾ; ʿ for ʿayn; ʾ for hamza; macron for long vowels (ā ī ū); double consonants for shadda
entries.standardEnglish: DMG / ALA-LC convention as the project standard for Arabic-source-text transliteration going forward
entries.wohChoice: preserved as the project-internal transliteration-convention; the translit field reflects the DMG / ALA-LC convention; sun-letters assimilated (al-shams becomes aš-šams; an-nās; ar-rabb); definite-article al- written joined when the next letter is a sun-letter and separated by a hyphen otherwise
entries.rationale:
**The WoH-Translation of the Qur'an adopts the DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) transliteration convention** with ALA-LC (American Library Association / Library of Congress) compatibility as the project-standard for Arabic source-text rendering. The convention uses standard underdot for emphatic consonants (ṣ for ṣād, ḍ for ḍād, ṭ for ṭāʾ, ẓ for ẓāʾ, ḥ for ḥāʾ); special diacritics for the sibilants and laterals (š for shīn, ḏ for ḏāl, ṯ for thāʾ, ḫ for the kh-sound, ġ for the gh-sound); ʿ for ʿayn; ʾ for hamza; macron for long vowels (ā, ī, ū); double consonants for shadda; sun-letters are assimilated in the article (aš-šams, an-nās, ar-rabb).

**The convention is the academic standard** in modern Quranic-studies and Islamic-studies publications, used by the *Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān* (Brill), the *Encyclopaedia of Islam* (Brill, 2nd and 3rd editions), the *Journal of Qur'anic Studies* (Edinburgh), and the *Corpus Coranicum* project. The convention is distinct from the popular-English transliteration conventions (which use 'th', 'kh', 'gh', 'sh' digraphs and capitalize divine names) and from the IJMES (International Journal of Middle East Studies) convention (which is similar but uses 'q' instead of 'ḳ' for qāf). The WoH-Translation's choice of DMG / ALA-LC aligns with the academic Quranic-studies tradition.

Named scholarship: **C. Brockelmann**, *Geschichte der arabischen Litteratur* (Leiden 1937-1949) — the foundational DMG-convention reference; **W. Wright**, *A Grammar of the Arabic Language*, 3rd ed. (Cambridge 1896-1898); **C. P. Caspari**, *Grammatica Arabica*; **ALA-LC Romanization Tables: Transliteration Schemes for Non-Roman Scripts* (Library of Congress 1997, with periodic updates); **DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) transliteration tables*; **Encyclopaedia of Islam**, 3rd ed. (Brill, ongoing); **Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān**, ed. J. D. McAuliffe (Brill 2001-2006); **Journal of Qur'anic Studies** (Edinburgh).

**Promotion candidate:** if subsequent WoH-Translation Islamic-tradition compositions adopt the DMG / ALA-LC convention, this overlay entry should be promoted to the central glossary as a project-wide convention.

entries.lemma: muḥdaṯ (Arabic; passive participle Form IV of ḥ-d-ṯ 'to be new, to come-to-be-newly'); the technical Quranic-term 'newly-given, newly-originated' at Sura 21:2 (also 26:5); the term carries a famous theological-history valence as the lexical-anchor of the Mu'tazila-vs-Ash'arī khalq al-Qurʾān 'createdness of the Qur'an' controversy under the Miḥna of al-Maʾmūn (827-848 CE)
entries.partOfSpeech: Quranic-theological technical term: 'newly-given / newly-originated'; the rendering choice carries a theological-history valence
entries.wohChoice: 'newly-given' (Sura 21:2) — theologically neutral, does not commit to either the Mu'tazila 'newly-created' (khalq al-Qurʾān) or the Ash'arī 'eternally-existing-but-revealed-in-time' position; the Miḥna controversy is documented in commentary but not adjudicated
entries.rationale:
**The Arabic *muḥdaṯ* at Sura 21:2 ('no newly-given reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while they are at play') carries a famous theological-history valence.** The lexical sense of *muḥdaṯ* (Form IV passive participle of ḥ-d-ṯ 'to be new, to come-to-be-newly') is 'newly-come-to-be / newly-originated / newly-given'; the rendering choice in English is the lexical-anchor of the famous *khalq al-Qurʾān* 'createdness of the Qur'an' controversy.

**The Miḥna controversy (827-848 CE).** The Caliph al-Maʾmūn instituted the *Miḥna* (the 'inquisition') in 218 AH / 833 CE, requiring the religious-scholarly establishment to profess the Mu'tazila doctrine of *khalq al-Qurʾān* — that the Qur'an is *muḥdaṯ* in the sense of 'created', i.e., not co-eternal with God. The Mu'tazila position was anchored in the rationalist-philosophical commitment to strict tawḥīd: anything other than God that is eternal would compromise the unity of God. The Ash'arī tradition (developed by al-Ashʿarī in the 10th c., grounded in the earlier Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal position) maintained that the Qur'an is the *kalām Allāh* 'speech of God' and as such is one of God's eternal attributes, not a created thing; the Sura-21:2 *muḥdaṯ* is read in the Ash'arī tradition as 'newly-revealed-in-time' (rather than 'newly-created'), preserving the eternal-Qur'an doctrine. The Miḥna was effectively reversed by al-Mutawakkil (846 CE), and the Ash'arī position became the mainstream Sunni position; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's resistance to the Miḥna is the foundational episode of the Sunni traditionalist tradition.

**The translator's default of 'newly-given' is theologically neutral.** It does not commit to either the Mu'tazila *khalq al-Qurʾān* reading ('newly-created') or the Ash'arī 'eternally-existing-but-newly-revealed-in-time' reading. The Anglophone-Quranic-translation tradition has variants: Asad ('fresh' — closer to the Mu'tazila side without explicit commitment); Pickthall ('new' — neutral); some translators use 'newly-revealed' (Ash'arī-leaning). The WoH-Translation preserves the theological-neutrality by rendering 'newly-given'.

Named scholarship: **W. Madelung**, 'The Origins of the Controversy concerning the Creation of the Koran', in J. M. Barral (ed.), *Orientalia Hispanica*, vol. 1 (Leiden: Brill 1974), 504-525 — the foundational modern study; **W. Madelung**, *Religious Trends in Early Islamic Iran* (Albany 1988); **J. van Ess**, *Theologie und Gesellschaft im 2. und 3. Jahrhundert Hidschra*, 6 vols. (Berlin: de Gruyter 1991-1997) — the foundational comprehensive study of early Islamic theology; **R. Caspar**, *Traité de théologie musulmane*, vol. 1 (Rome 1987); **A. S. Tritton**, *Muslim Theology* (London: Luzac 1947); **W. Watt**, *Islamic Philosophy and Theology* (Edinburgh 1962); **G. Hourani**, *Islamic Rationalism: The Ethics of ʿAbd al-Jabbār* (Oxford 1971); **A. K. Reinhart**, *Before Revelation: The Boundaries of Muslim Moral Thought* (Albany 1995); **C. Melchert**, *Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal* (Oxford 2006); **al-Ṭabarī**, *Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk* (the historical narrative of the Miḥna); **al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī**, *Tārīkh Baghdād* (the prosopographical narrative).

**Promotion candidate:** if subsequent WoH-Translation Islamic-tradition compositions activate the Miḥna controversy or the khalq al-Qurʾān doctrine, this overlay entry should be promoted to the central glossary as a project-wide convention.

entries.lemma: the two principal early Hijazi-script manuscript witnesses for the WoH-Translation of the Qur'an: (1) Tübingen Fragment Ma VI 165 — radiocarbon-dated 649-675 CE; contains Suras 17-36; source for Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:1-5; held at Tübingen University Library; (2) Codex Parisino-petropolitanus — BnF Arabe 328 + St. Petersburg / Birmingham / Vatican fragments; late 7th c. CE Hijazi script; source for Sūrat al-Qamar 54:1 and Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah 56:15-24; BnF in Paris, with related fragments at the National Library of Russia (St. Petersburg), Cadbury Research Library Birmingham, and the BAV Vatican
entries.standardEnglish: Tübingen Ma VI 165; Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328)
entries.wohChoice: preserved as the paleographic-source-of-record for the WoH-Translation of the Qur'an; verification of the precise letter-skeleton against the original codicology is pending; the rasm field reflects the early-manuscript orthography to the extent reconstructable from published facsimiles and the Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus
entries.rationale:
**The WoH-Translation of the Qur'an is sourced from two principal early Hijazi-script manuscript witnesses.**

**(1) Tübingen Fragment Ma VI 165.** Held at Tübingen University Library (Universitätsbibliothek Tübingen, Ma VI 165). Hijazi script. Radiocarbon-dated 649-675 CE (within 17-43 years of the traditional Uthmanic codification c. 650 CE). Contains Suras 17 (al-Isrāʾ) through 36 (Yā Sīn). Source for Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:1-5 in the WoH-Translation. The radiocarbon dating was performed by ETH Zurich in 2014 and reported in the press by the Tübingen University Library (the press-release framed it as 'one of the oldest Qur'an manuscripts in the world').

**(2) Codex Parisino-petropolitanus.** A dispersed codex whose principal extant fragments are: BnF Arabe 328 (Paris; the largest portion), with related fragments at the National Library of Russia (St. Petersburg, the 'petropolitanus' part of the name), the Cadbury Research Library Birmingham (the Mingana fragment), and the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana (Rome). Hijazi script, late 7th c. CE. Source for Sūrat al-Qamar 54:1 and Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah 56:15-24 in the WoH-Translation. The codicological reconstruction is the work of **F. Déroche**, *La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus* (Leiden: Brill 2009).

**The verification status** of the WoH-Translation source-rendering is 'best-effort reconstruction; verification pending against the original manuscript codicology and the full Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 / Hilali 2017 / Déroche 2009/2014 apparatus'. The rasm field in the source-ar-N.json and chapter-N.json files reflects the early-manuscript orthography to the extent reconstructable from published facsimiles and the Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus; verification against the original codicology at Tübingen UB, BnF Paris, National Library of Russia St. Petersburg, Cadbury Research Library Birmingham, and BAV Vatican is pending.

**The manuscript-criticism context** is genuinely scholarly-contested. The **Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 thesis** ('Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān', *Der Islam* 87, 1-129) frames the early manuscripts as evidence of an early canonical text with limited variation; the **Hilali 2017 thesis** (*The Sanaa Palimpsest: The Transmission of the Qur'an in the First Centuries AH*, Oxford) frames the Sanʿāʾ 1 palimpsest evidence as showing 'transmission in flux' during the first century AH; earlier scholarship (**Wansbrough 1977**, *Quranic Studies*, Oxford; **Crone-Cook 1977**, *Hagarism*, Cambridge) proposed later-canonization frameworks that the more recent manuscript discoveries have substantially nuanced. The WoH-Translation preserves the textual-criticism dispute rather than adjudicating it.

Named scholarship: **B. Sadeghi and U. Bergmann**, 'The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet', *Arabica* 57 (2010), 343-436; **B. Sadeghi and M. Goudarzi**, 'Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān', *Der Islam* 87 (2010), 1-129; **A. Hilali**, *The Sanaa Palimpsest: The Transmission of the Qur'an in the First Centuries AH* (Oxford 2017); **F. Déroche**, *Qur'ans of the Umayyads* (Brill 2014); *La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus* (Brill 2009); **F. Déroche**, *The Abbasid Tradition* (London 1992); **A. Neuwirth**, *Scripture, Poetry, and the Making of a Community* (Oxford 2014); **J. Wansbrough**, *Quranic Studies* (Oxford 1977); **P. Crone and M. Cook**, *Hagarism* (Cambridge 1977); **G. S. Reynolds** (ed.), *The Qurʾān in Its Historical Context* (Routledge 2008/2011, 2 vols); **Corpus Coranicum** project (Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities).

**Promotion candidate:** the manuscript-attestation reference does not have direct cross-corpus reach to non-Quranic texts and is therefore appropriate as an overlay entry rather than a central-glossary entry.
